text.p: Australian winemakers said the 1997 vintage was looking good, with an anticipated 825,000 tonnes of grapes to be crushed, given the stock levels resulting from the record 1996 885,000 tonnes vintage.
Winemakers' Federation of Australia president Stephen Shelmerdine said in a statement high stock levels would impact on grape prices and a levelling out of prices was expected.
"Demand for premium red wine will continue to outstrip supply as a reduced vintage is experienced because northern hemisphere vintages have been unremarkable," he said.

Shelmerdine said in the year to the end of November domestic bottled table wine sales were up 7.1 percent on a moving annual total (MAT) basis, with white wine up 2.1 percent to 52.3 million litres and red wine up 15.8 percent to 35.7 million litres.

Sparkling wine sales had grown by 10.1 percent to 31.3 million litres and cask wine by three percent to 163 million litres, amounting to an overall growth of 3.8 percent on a MAT of 319.8 million litres, he said.
Export markets were showing strong growth by volume, up 28.8 percent to 145.7 million litres and value, up 38.7 percent to A$543 million on a MAT basis, he said.

Shelmerdine said while the industry welcomed the new Federal government's policy on low inflation and low interest growth as a deficit reduction strategy, the first eight months of dealing with a new minister had been disappointing.

Key issues relating to an export levy and the amalgamation of two industry bodies remained unresolved, while the government had rejected proposed industry candidates for the head of a key body and cancelled cash grants to smaller winemakers, he said.
"Thus far, on specific wine industry issues, the new Federal government is batting zero out of four," he said.
